teile.einleitung: After the African elephant, the Asian elephant is the largest land animal on Earth. It lives in the forests and grasslands of South and South-East Asia. For thousands of years people have worked together with tamed Asian elephants.
wichtigste: The scientific name of the Asian elephant is Elephas maximus.
It lives in the wild in South and South-East Asia.
It has smaller ears than the African elephant and a forehead with two bulges.
A grown-up elephant eats over 100 kilograms of food a day.
A newborn calf weighs about 100 kilograms and first drinks its mother's milk.
Adult males mostly live alone or in small bachelor groups.
The species is highly endangered.

abschnitte.text: Asian elephants grow to about 3 metres tall, and the bulls weigh up to around 5 tonnes. Compared with African elephants they have smaller, rounded **ears**. Their forehead has two bulges, and the highest point of the body is the arched back. At the tip of the trunk they have only one finger-like projection, while African elephants have two. Only some of the bulls carry long **tusks**, and the cows have at most small tusklets.

The Asian elephant lives in the wild in South and South-East Asia, for example in India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Malaysia and on Sumatra and Borneo. It feels at home in **forests** and grassland with water. Around 50,000 wild animals are still alive worldwide, most of them in India. Their habitat is often cut up into small pieces.

Elephants are pure **plant eaters**. A grown-up Asian elephant eats over 100 kilograms of grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit every day. It spends up to 18 hours a day busy eating. It also drinks a lot of water and likes to bathe. When swimming, it can use its trunk as a snorkel under water.

Females and young live in **herds** led by an experienced lead cow. Adult males mostly live alone or in small bachelor groups. An elephant cow is pregnant for about 22 months, longer than any other mammal. A newborn calf weighs about 100 kilograms and at first feeds on its mother's milk.

Tame Asian elephants used often to be used for carrying heavy **tree trunks** in the forest. They also played a role in wars and at religious festivals, for example at the Perahera festival in Sri Lanka. Today there are often conflicts when wild elephants raid fields. That is why in some countries people protect their fields with fences and ditches.

The Asian elephant is listed on the Red List as **endangered**. Threats are the loss of habitat, poaching for ivory and conflicts with people. In Switzerland you can see Asian elephants at Zurich Zoo, which opened the large **Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park** in 2014. The facility is named after a national park in Thailand.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long, flexible extension of an elephant's nose and upper lip.
Greatly lengthened incisor teeth made of ivory.
The oldest and most experienced elephant cow, who leads the herd.
A male elephant.

gewusst: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles, but not a single bone.
Elephants can recognise themselves in a mirror, which only a few animals can do.
Asian elephants also communicate with very low sounds that people cannot hear.

teile.einleitung: The woodlouse hunter is a spider that specialises in hunting woodlice. This means the woodlouse spiders of the genus Dysdera, above all the common woodlouse spider. With their huge fangs they pierce the hard armour of their prey.
wichtigste: Woodlouse spiders of the genus Dysdera specialise in hunting woodlice.
The best-known species is the common woodlouse spider, Dysdera crocata.
They have strikingly large fangs.
Their front body and legs are reddish brown, the abdomen is pale.
They have only six eyes instead of eight.
Woodlouse spiders do not build a catching web, but hunt at night on the ground.
They are harmless to people.

abschnitte.text: The **common woodlouse spider** grows to about 1 to 1.5 centimetres long, depending on its sex. The front body and legs are a strong reddish brown, the abdomen is pale grey to beige. Striking are the large, forward-pointing **chelicerae**, the fangs. Woodlouse spiders have six eyes that stand close together.

Woodlouse spiders live under stones, pieces of wood, bark and leaves, where it is damp. That is exactly where woodlice like to stay, too. The common woodlouse spider comes from the Mediterranean region, but has been carried by people to many parts of the world. It also occurs in Switzerland, often in gardens and sometimes in cellars.

**Woodlice** are small crustaceans with a hard, armoured back that many other predators avoid. Woodlouse spiders seize a woodlouse with their long fangs and stab one fang from below into the soft belly. The other fang often pierces the armour on the back. Besides woodlice, they also eat other small ground animals.

Woodlouse spiders are **nocturnal** and only go hunting in the dark. They do not build a catching web. They spend the day in a small, sack-like hiding place made of spider silk. The females also lay their eggs in such a silk sack and guard them.

Woodlouse spiders are not dangerous to people. If you pick them up, however, they can bite with their strong jaws. It feels like a needle prick and can itch or swell briefly. It is best to leave them alone, because they are useful residents of the garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fangs of a spider, with which it bites and injects venom.
A small crustacean with armour that lives on land in damp places.
An animal that is mainly on the move at night.
A group of very closely related species, here the genus Dysdera.

gewusst: The common woodlouse spider belongs to the family of six-eyed spiders.
Some species of the genus Dysdera have differently shaped jaws, depending on how they seize woodlice.
On the Canary Islands there are especially many different Dysdera species.

teile.einleitung: The Atlantic salmon is a powerful migratory fish that grows up in the sea and returns to its home river to spawn. On this journey it even leaps over waterfalls. In the past it swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Atlantic salmon is called Salmo salar scientifically and belongs to the bony fish.
It can grow to about 1.5 metres long.
Young salmon grow up in the river, adults live in the sea.
To spawn they migrate back to their home river and find it mainly by their sense of smell.
They often overcome waterfalls and weirs with powerful leaps.
In the past the Rhine was an important salmon river as far as Switzerland.
Norway is one of the biggest producers of farmed salmon.

abschnitte.text: The Atlantic salmon, in Latin **Salmo salar**, is a bony fish from the salmon family. It has a slim, silvery shiny body with small black spots. Large animals grow to about 1.5 metres long, but most stay considerably smaller. At spawning time the males turn reddish, and their lower jaw curves into a hook, and they are then called **hook-jawed salmon**.

Salmon hatch in gravelly rivers in the north of Europe and North America. The young fish are called **parr** and have dark marks on their sides that camouflage them well on the stream bed. After one to several years they turn silvery and swim to the sea. In the North Atlantic they eat mainly small fish and crustaceans and grow quickly.

After one or more years in the sea the salmon return to the river where they were born. This journey is called the **spawning migration**, and they recognise their home river mainly by its smell. On the way they overcome waterfalls and weirs with leaps of over a metre in height. During the migration they hardly eat anything and live on their fat reserves. Many animals die after spawning, but some return to the sea and spawn once more later.

In the sea, seals, large predatory fish and seabirds hunt the salmon. In the river otters, bears and herons are dangerous. Even greater are the problems caused by humans, such as **dams**, polluted water and overfishing. That is why wild salmon have become rare in many rivers.

Until the 19th century many salmon swam up the **Rhine** every year as far as Basel and on into the Aare and Limmat. Through the building of power stations, straightening of rivers and dirty water, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland in the 20th century. Today the countries along the Rhine are working to make the power stations passable with **fish ladders** so that the salmon can return. In Switzerland young salmon have already been released into streams for this purpose.

Almost all the salmon that you can buy in the shop comes from **aquaculture**. Norway is one of the largest producers, and Scotland and Chile also farm a lot of salmon. The fish grow up there in large net pens in the sea. Critics complain that diseases and escaped farmed salmon can harm the wild salmon.

begriffe.erklaerung: Laying eggs and fertilising them, in fish and amphibians.
A young salmon with dark marks that still lives in the river.
A male salmon at spawning time with a curved lower jaw.
A structure with steps and pools by which fish can swim around a weir.
The farming of fish or other water animals by people.

gewusst: The pink colour of salmon flesh comes from pigments in the crustaceans that the salmon eats.
In Basel there are said to have been so many salmon in the past that they counted as simple everyday food.
On its spawning migration a salmon can swim more than a thousand kilometres upstream.

teile.einleitung: Anadromy is a technical word for a special migration of fish. Anadromous fish grow up in the sea and swim up rivers to spawn, often into the very river where they were hatched themselves. The best-known example is the salmon.
wichtigste: Anadromous fish live in the sea and migrate into rivers to spawn.
The word comes from Greek and means roughly “running up”.
Typical anadromous fish are salmon, sea trout, allis shad, sturgeon and sea lamprey.
The opposite is called catadromous, as with the eel.
Salmon find their home river mainly with their sense of smell.
Dams and power stations block the way for many migratory fish.
In the past, salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Anadromy** means a migration from the sea upstream into fresh water in order to spawn there. The word is made up of the Greek parts ana, “up”, and dromos, “run”. The eggs are laid in rivers and streams, where the young fish hatch. Later the young fish migrate to the sea, where they find plenty of food and grow large. Fish with such migrations are called **migratory fish**.

The best-known example is the **Atlantic salmon**. Sea trout, allis shad, smelt, various **sturgeons** and the sea lamprey are also anadromous. In the Pacific there are several species of salmon, such as the sockeye and the Chinook. Pacific salmon die after spawning, while Atlantic salmon can return to the sea several times. In North America the dead salmon are an important food for bears and even fertilise the forests along the banks.

Salmon often live in the sea for several years and cover thousands of kilometres there. To spawn they usually return to exactly the river where they hatched. In the sea they probably find their way by the Earth's **magnetic field**. Near the coast they recognise their home river by the **smell** of the water. On the way upstream, salmon leap over rapids and small waterfalls.

abschnitte.titel: From salt water to fresh water
abschnitte.text: The change between sea and river is a great challenge for the body. In the sea a fish loses water, in fresh water it takes in too much water. Anadromous fish therefore adjust their gills and kidneys each time, which is called **osmoregulation**. Before their journey to the sea, young salmon even change colour and turn silvery. At this stage they are called smolts.

For **catadromous** fish it is exactly the other way round: they live in fresh water and spawn in the sea. The best-known example is the **European eel**. It grows up in rivers and lakes, including in Switzerland, and swims all the way to the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic to spawn. Both kinds of migration are grouped together under the term diadromous.

In the past, many salmon swam up the Rhine every year as far as Basel and on into the Aare, Limmat and Reuss. Because of **power stations**, weirs and polluted water, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland in the middle of the 20th century. Today the countries along the Rhine are building **fish ladders** and fish passes so that migratory fish can get past the obstacles. Young salmon are released into Swiss streams so that one day the salmon will return. But until salmon from the sea swim into Switzerland regularly again, more fish passes are still needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The laying of eggs by fish and amphibians.
A fish that travels back and forth between different bodies of water.
Living in fresh water and migrating to the sea to spawn, like the eel.
A structure with small pools that lets fish get around a weir or power station.

gewusst: Salmon can leap up waterfalls more than three metres high.
A single salmon can swim thousands of kilometres to return to the stream where it was born.
The sturgeon is an anadromous fish whose ancestors lived more than 100 million years ago.

teile.einleitung: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben are a well-known Swiss breed of chicken with a striking, pointed crest of feathers on the head. They come from the Appenzell region and are among the oldest breeds of chicken in Switzerland. With their cheeky tuft of feathers they look as if they were wearing a little hat.
wichtigste: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben is a well-known Swiss breed of chicken.
Typical is the pointed crest of feathers pointing forwards.
It comes from the Appenzell region in eastern Switzerland.
Instead of a large comb it has a small V-shaped comb.
The hens lay white eggs.
The chickens are light, hardy and good fliers.
Pro Specie Rara helps to preserve the breed.

abschnitte.text: The most striking feature is the pointed **crest of feathers** on the head, pointing forwards. Instead of a serrated comb the birds have a small, two-part **V-shaped comb** that looks like a V. The best-known colour is silver-spangled black, but there are also golden, black and blue birds. The chickens are slim and light and walk with a proud, upright gait.

The breed comes from the **Appenzell region** in eastern Switzerland and has been kept there for centuries. Its name comes from the Spitzhaube, a cap that used to be part of the traditional costume of Appenzell women. The chickens' crest of feathers is reminiscent of this headgear. This makes it a true Swiss breed of chicken.

A hen lays about 150 to 180 white eggs a year. A hen usually weighs only about 1.5 kilograms, a cockerel a little more. The breed is therefore not suited to producing a lot of meat. Today it is bred mainly by hobby keepers for its beauty and hardiness.

Appenzeller Spitzhauben are lively, curious and watchful chickens. They are very **hardy** and cope well with the rough mountain climate. Because they are light, they can fly well and like to perch in trees or on fences. They need plenty of room to roam, where they can scratch about and look for worms and grains.

In the 20th century the old native breeds became rarer and rarer, because high-performance chickens lay more eggs. Since the 1980s the foundation **Pro Specie Rara** has been working to preserve old Swiss breeds of farm animals, including the Appenzeller Spitzhauben. Thanks to dedicated breeders the breed is now secure again. At poultry shows in Switzerland it is a popular eye-catcher.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals of the same species with shared, bred characteristics.
A tuft of long feathers on the head of a bird.
A small comb made of two points that look like little horns.
A Swiss foundation that preserves old breeds of farm animals and cultivated plants.

gewusst: The crest of feathers can be so big that it takes away a little of the chickens' view.
There is a second Appenzell breed of chicken, the Appenzeller Barthuhn, which has a beard of feathers.
Appenzeller Spitzhauben fly so well that their run often has to be covered with a net.

teile.einleitung: The harlequin ladybird, also called the Asian ladybird, is a beetle from East Asia that is now also widespread in Switzerland. It was brought to Europe to fight aphids and then spread by itself in the wild. There it can push out native species of ladybird.
wichtigste: The harlequin ladybird comes from East Asia.
It has moved into Switzerland and can push out native species.
It is also called the Asian ladybird.
It was used to fight aphids.
Its colours and the number of spots vary a great deal.
In autumn it often seeks shelter in houses in large groups.
It also eats the larvae of other ladybirds.

abschnitte.text: The harlequin ladybird is about 5 to 8 millimetres long, and so a little bigger than many native species. Its colour varies a lot: yellow, orange, red or black with red spots. It can have no spots at all or up to about 20. Often there is a typical pale marking behind the head that looks like an **M** or a **W**. Because of this colourful variety it is also called the **harlequin ladybird**.

Its home is **East Asia**, for example China, Japan and Korea. Because it eats very many aphids, it was used in North America and Europe as a beneficial insect in greenhouses. From there it got out into the open and spread strongly. In Switzerland it was first recorded in the wild in 2004, and today it occurs almost everywhere on the Central Plateau.

The harlequin ladybird is a great **aphid eater**, and one larva eats hundreds of aphids. If it and its larvae find too few aphids, they also eat the eggs and larvae of other ladybirds. In this way it competes with native species such as the **seven-spot ladybird**. In autumn it also likes to eat ripe, sweet fruit such as grapes.

In autumn the beetles often gather in their hundreds on bright house walls. They creep through cracks in window frames and spend the winter in houses and attics. They are harmless to people, but can sometimes give a slight nip. When in danger they release a yellow, bad-smelling liquid that can leave stains.

Because the harlequin ladybird multiplies so strongly, it counts as an **invasive species**. It also brings a fungal parasite that is harmless to itself but can harm native species. In vineyards, beetles that are pressed with the grapes can give the wine an unpleasant taste. Today it is no longer released as a beneficial insect in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: An introduced living thing that spreads strongly and pushes out native species.
An animal that eats pests and so helps people.
A tiny insect that sucks plant sap.
A colourful jester figure from the theatre, after which the beetle is named.

gewusst: For defence, ladybirds release bitter drops from the joints of their legs, which is called reflex bleeding.
A single harlequin ladybird can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime.
Because it can reproduce several times a year, the harlequin ladybird quickly becomes common.

teile.einleitung: An aquarium is a glass container of water in which you keep fish, plants and other water animals and can watch them. To keep the animals well, an aquarium needs plants, a filter and regular care. Large public aquariums even show sharks, rays and whole underwater worlds.
wichtigste: An aquarium is a small, artificial habitat under water.
There are freshwater aquariums and marine aquariums.
Plants produce oxygen and give the fish shelter.
A pump or a filter with aeration provides enough oxygen.
Fish need plants or other hiding places where they can retreat.
The water should be partly changed regularly, for example every week.
Goldfish need a large tank and company of their own kind.

abschnitte.text: The word **aquarium** comes from the Latin “aqua” for water. It means a container, usually made of glass, in which water creatures are kept. In a **freshwater aquarium** live fish from rivers and lakes, such as goldfish, guppies or neon tetras. In a **marine aquarium** swim animals from the sea, for example clownfish among corals.

A **filter** sucks in water, cleans it of dirt and returns it. A pump or a filter with aeration makes sure that enough oxygen gets into the water. Tropical fish also need a heater, while goldfish prefer cool water. A lamp replaces sunlight so that the plants can grow.

Water plants are very important in an aquarium. They produce oxygen and take waste substances out of the water. At the same time, plants, stones and roots give the fish **hiding places** where they can rest and feel safe. Without places to retreat to, many fish become stressed and ill.

Fish release waste into the water, which becomes poisonous over time. Useful **bacteria** in the filter turn these substances into less harmful ones. Even so, you should change part of the water regularly, for example every week. A new aquarium must first run for a few weeks without fish so that these bacteria can settle in.

Goldfish come from **China**, where they have been bred for over a thousand years. They can live for many years and grow to over 20 centimetres long. Small round bowls are therefore completely unsuitable for them. Goldfish are sociable and should never live alone, and in summer they also feel at home in a garden pond.

Public aquariums show animals from rivers, lakes and oceans. In Switzerland **Aquatis** in Lausanne is well known. It opened in 2017 and is one of the largest freshwater aquariums in Europe. Basel Zoo, too, has a large aquarium complex in its Vivarium. Such aquariums help to get people excited about protecting waters.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that cleans and moves the water in the aquarium.
Replacing only part of the water instead of emptying the whole tank.
Water from rivers and lakes that contains hardly any salt.
A gas that fish take from the water with their gills and need to live.

gewusst: With good care, goldfish can live for more than 20 years.
The first public aquariums appeared around 1850 in England.
Fish have no eyelids and therefore sleep with their eyes open.

teile.einleitung: Anemonefish, also called clownfish, are small, colourful fish from coral reefs. They live among the poisonous tentacles of sea anemones without being hurt. Through the film “Finding Nemo” they have become world famous.
wichtigste: Anemonefish live in warm coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
There are about 30 species.
They live in partnership with sea anemones.
A layer of mucus protects them from the anemone's stinging poison.
All anemonefish hatch as males.
The largest fish in a group is the female.
If the female dies, the largest male becomes the female.

abschnitte.text: Anemonefish are usually only 6 to 15 centimetres long. Many are orange, red, yellow or black and have broad **white stripes**. The best known is the false clownfish, which looks like Nemo in the film. In all there are about 30 species. They belong to the damselfish family.

Anemonefish live in warm, shallow **coral reefs** in the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea and the western Pacific. They do not occur in the wild in the Atlantic. Each group lives in its own sea anemone and hardly ever strays far from it. The anemone is their home, hiding place and nursery. They mainly eat plankton, small crustaceans and algae.

Sea anemones have many tentacles with **stinging cells** that paralyse small fish. Anemonefish are protected by a special **layer of mucus** on their skin. Among the tentacles they are safe from predatory fish. In return they defend the anemone against enemies, clean it and supply it with nutrients from their droppings. Such a partnership for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**.

All anemonefish hatch as males. In one anemone lives a group with a fixed pecking order. The largest fish is the **female**, the second largest is the only male that breeds. If the female dies, the male changes into a female, and a younger male moves up. This change of sex from male to female is called **protandry**.

The female lays hundreds of eggs on a stone right next to the anemone. The male guards the eggs, fans fresh water over them and removes spoiled eggs. After about a week the tiny larvae hatch and drift in the sea. Later the young fish look for an anemone, which they probably find with their sense of smell.

Since the film “Finding Nemo” in 2003, anemonefish have been very popular as **aquarium fish**. Many animals used to be caught in the sea, but today most are bred. Anemonefish are threatened mainly by the warming of the seas and **coral bleaching**, which also weakens anemones. You can watch anemonefish in Swiss zoos and show aquariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two different species living together in a way that benefits both.
Tiny poison capsules that jellyfish and anemones use to paralyse their prey.
A change of sex in which an animal is first male and later female.
An underwater ridge made from the limestone skeletons of tiny coral animals.

gewusst: In real life, Nemo's father would himself have become a female after the mother's death.
Anemonefish can make popping and clicking sounds to communicate.

teile.einleitung: Anubis is a deity of ancient Egypt who is shown with the body of a man and the head of a jackal. He was responsible for mummification and for accompanying the dead. His image links the religion of the Egyptians with a real wild animal of the desert.
wichtigste: Anubis is a god of ancient Egypt with a jackal's head.
He was responsible for mummification and for accompanying the dead.
The model was a dog-like predator that lived on the edge of the desert.
Today this animal is regarded as the African golden wolf and no longer as a true jackal.
Anubis was often painted entirely black, because black stood for fertile earth and new life.
At the judgement of the dead, Anubis weighed the heart of the deceased on a pair of scales.
The olive baboon is also named after Anubis.

abschnitte.titel: A god with an animal's head
abschnitte.text: The ancient Egyptians showed many of their gods with animal heads. Anubis has the slim head of a **jackal** with a long snout and pointed, upright ears. Sometimes he was also shown as a black dog lying on a chest. Such figures often stood at tomb entrances and were meant to guard the dead.

Anubis was regarded as the inventor of **mummification**, that is, the art of preserving the dead. The priests who embalmed the dead sometimes wore a mask with his head. The Egyptians believed that the body had to be preserved so that the soul could go on living in the afterlife. That is why Anubis was especially important to them.

According to Egyptian belief, every dead person had to appear before a court. Anubis placed the heart of the deceased on a pair of scales. On the other side lay a feather of the goddess **Maat**, who stood for truth and order. If the heart was no heavier than the feather, the soul was allowed to go on into the afterlife. This scene is often painted in the Egyptian **Book of the Dead**.

On the edge of the desert, dog-like predators roamed around the cemeteries looking for food. Perhaps that is why the Egyptians came up with the idea of making such an animal the protecting god of the dead. For a long time this animal was called the golden jackal. Genetic studies showed in 2015 that the animals in North Africa are a species of their own, the **African golden wolf**.

Many statues and wall paintings of Anubis have survived and can be seen in museums all over the world. A black, reclining figure of Anubis from the tomb of **Tutankhamun** is famous, and is now displayed in Egypt. Anubis also often appears in books, films and games. In Switzerland you can see Egyptian art, for example, in the Museum of Ancient Art in Basel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A god or goddess, that is, a being worshipped in a religion.
Preserving a dead body with salt, oils and linen bandages.
The world in which, according to the belief of many people, the soul goes on living after death.
A dog-like predator from North Africa that used to be thought of as a jackal.

gewusst: The ancient Greeks called the city where Anubis was especially worshipped “Kynopolis”, which means City of Dogs.
The black colour of Anubis had nothing to do with mourning, but stood for the fertile mud of the Nile.
In Egypt thousands of dogs were mummified and buried as offerings to Anubis.

teile.einleitung: Anacondas are giant constrictor snakes from South America that spend a large part of their lives in the water. The green anaconda is regarded as the heaviest snake in the world. It is not venomous, but crushes its prey with its powerful body.
wichtigste: Anacondas belong to the genus Eunectes in the boa family.
Eunectes means “good swimmer” in Ancient Greek.
The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.
Anacondas live in swamps, rivers and floodplains of South America.
They are not venomous and kill their prey by squeezing.
Anacondas give birth to live young.
In 2024 it was proposed to split the green anaconda into a northern and a southern species.

abschnitte.text: Anacondas make up the genus **Eunectes**, which means “good swimmer” in Ancient Greek. They belong to the boa family (Boidae). The best known are the giant or **green anaconda**, the smaller yellow anaconda and a few other, rare species. Carl Linnaeus was the first to describe the giant anaconda scientifically in 1758, then under the name Boa murina. Its species name murinus is usually interpreted today as “hunting mice”.

The green anaconda is olive green with large, dark spots. Its eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head, so it can breathe and look almost completely underwater. Females are much larger than males and can grow to over five metres long and weigh well over 70 kilograms. This makes it the **heaviest snake** in the world. The longest snake, however, is the reticulated python from Asia.

Anacondas live in tropical **South America** east of the Andes. They are found in the Amazon region, in the Orinoco basin, in the Llanos of Venezuela and Colombia, and the yellow anaconda in the Pantanal. They like slow-flowing rivers, swamps and flooded grasslands. In the water they move elegantly, on land they seem rather clumsy. In dry seasons they sometimes bury themselves in the mud.

Anacondas are **constrictors** and are not venomous. They lie in wait in the water, grab their prey with their mouth and coil around it in a flash. Then they squeeze until the animal dies, and swallow it whole. Large anacondas eat fish, birds, capybaras, caimans and even deer. After a large meal they often do not need to eat again for weeks.

At mating time, several males sometimes coil around one female at the same time, which is called a **mating ball**. Anacondas do not lay eggs but give birth to live young. A female usually gives birth to 20 to 40 young snakes, which are already more than half a metre long. The young are independent from the start and have to watch out for caimans and birds of prey.

The word **anaconda** originally referred to snakes in Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon. According to one theory it comes from a Tamil expression meaning “elephant killer”. A study from 2024 showed that the northern and southern green anacondas differ by about 5.5 per cent in their mitochondrial DNA. Their lines separated about 10 million years ago. For the northern green anaconda the name **Eunectes akayima** was therefore proposed, and akayima means “big snake”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A snake that coils around its prey and crushes it instead of poisoning it.
A group of closely related species, for example all the anacondas.
The young are born fully developed and do not hatch from eggs in a nest.
The blueprint of a living thing, which is found in every cell.

gewusst: After a large meal, a female anaconda can fast for months.
Anacondas can stay underwater for about ten minutes without breathing.
Female anacondas sometimes eat a male after mating, because they need a lot of energy for the long pregnancy.

teile.einleitung: Woodlice are small, grey animals with seven pairs of legs that you find under stones, leaves and wood. Although they live on land, they are not insects but crustaceans. In the garden they do important work as nature's refuse collectors.
wichtigste: Woodlice are crustaceans and form the order Isopoda, the “equal-footed” ones.
A full-grown land woodlouse has seven pairs of legs that look quite alike.
Land woodlice need moisture and are therefore mostly active at night and at dusk.
They break down dead plant parts and so help to form fertile humus.
The female carries her eggs in a brood pouch on her belly.
Woodlice are completely harmless to people, they can neither sting nor bite.

abschnitte.text: Woodlice are related to crabs and lobsters and belong to the **crustaceans**. The order is called **Isopoda**, in German “Gleichfüsser”, because their legs all look quite alike. Worldwide more than 10,000 species are known, most of which live in the sea or in fresh water. Land woodlice are one of the few groups of crustaceans that have conquered the land.

The body of a woodlouse is flat and covered with hard plates that look like armour. A grown-up land woodlouse walks on seven pairs of legs, and at the front it has two pairs of **antennae**, one of which is tiny. Well-known species in Switzerland are the **common rough woodlouse** and the common shiny woodlouse, which usually grow to one to two centimetres long. The pill woodlouse can roll itself up into a ball when in danger. When a woodlouse grows, it moults in two steps, first the rear and then the front half of the body.

Land woodlice breathe with gill-like organs on their rear legs, which have to stay moist. That is why during the day they hide under stones, bark, leaves or in cellars and only come out at night and at dusk. They often gather in **groups**, because it stays damper there and they are better protected. In dry air they would quickly dry out.

Woodlice eat mainly dead leaves, rotting wood and other plant remains. In doing so they break up the material, and their droppings are broken down further by bacteria and fungi. This produces **humus**, that is, fertile soil in which new plants grow well. Anyone who wants to encourage woodlice in the garden makes heaps of leaves and piles of dead wood and stones.

The female carries her eggs in a **brood pouch** on her belly, which is filled with liquid. The young hatch inside it and only leave the pouch as tiny, fully formed woodlice. Young woodlice at first have only six pairs of legs, and the seventh comes after the first moult. Their enemies include spiders, ground beetles, hedgehogs, shrews and birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with a hard shell to which crabs, lobsters and also woodlice belong.
The scientific name of woodlice, meaning equal-footed.
Dark, fertile soil that forms from broken-down plant and animal remains.
A pouch on the female's belly in which the eggs and young grow.

gewusst: The largest woodlice in the world live in the deep sea and can grow to about 50 centimetres long.
Woodlice moult in two halves, so you sometimes see animals that are pale at the back and dark at the front.
Woodlice do not only drink with their mouth, but can also take in water through their rear end.

teile.einleitung: Arthropleura was a giant, millipede-like arthropod that lived about 300 million years ago. It grew to more than two metres long and is regarded as the largest arthropod that ever lived on land. You can imagine it as a millipede as long as a car is wide.
wichtigste: Arthropleura was a prehistoric arthropod.
It grew to more than two metres long.
It lived in the Carboniferous and early Permian, about 345 to 290 million years ago.
It is related to today's millipedes.
Fossils have been found in Europe and North America.
It was the largest known land invertebrate of all time.
It probably fed mainly on plants.

abschnitte.text: Arthropleura was an **arthropod**, that is, an animal with an outer skeleton and jointed legs, like insects, spiders and crustaceans. Its body consisted of about 30 segments with armour plates. It was flat and broad and could grow to over two metres long and about half a metre wide. This makes it the largest known **invertebrate** that ever lived on land.

Arthropleura lived in the **Carboniferous** and the early Permian, about 345 to 290 million years ago. At that time a large part of Europe and North America lay near the equator. There were huge, damp swamp forests with tree-sized club mosses and horsetails. Coal later formed from these forests.

Complete skeletons of Arthropleura are very rare, and usually only parts of the armour are found. More common are fossilised **trackways**, that is, traces of its many legs in the mud. In 2018 an especially large piece of armour was discovered on the coast of northern England, which could have come from an animal about 2.6 metres long. At the end of 2024 researchers described for the first time well-preserved heads from France, which confirmed the relationship with the **millipedes**.

What Arthropleura ate is not entirely certain. Many researchers think it fed mainly on plant remains, spores and seeds. Perhaps it also ate smaller animals or carrion. Such a large animal probably had hardly any big enemies at that time.

In the Carboniferous the air contained more **oxygen** than today, by estimates more than 30 per cent instead of about 21 per cent. This may have made breathing easier for large arthropods. Relatives of dragonflies with wingspans of around 70 centimetres also lived then. In addition, there were not yet any large land vertebrates that competed with them for food or living space.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals with a hard outer shell and jointed legs, for example insects and spiders.
A period in the history of the Earth about 359 to 299 million years ago with large swamp forests.
Turned-to-stone remains or traces of living things from prehistoric times.
Without a backbone, like insects, worms or snails.

gewusst: Arthropleura was longer than a grown-up person is tall.
The name Arthropleura means roughly jointed sides.
Its tracks are sometimes almost half a metre wide.

teile.einleitung: The olive baboon is a large species of monkey from Africa that is named after the Egyptian god Anubis. Its long, dog-like snout is reminiscent of the god's jackal head. It lives in large groups and is the most widespread species of baboon.
wichtigste: The olive baboon is also called the Anubis baboon, after the Egyptian god Anubis.
Because of its olive-greenish fur it is also called the green baboon.
It lives in a broad belt across Africa south of the Sahara.
Olive baboons live in groups that often number several dozen animals.
They eat almost anything: grass, fruit, seeds, insects and small animals.
The males are much larger than the females and have a mane.
The species is not considered endangered today.

abschnitte.text: The olive baboon has dense, grey-brown fur with an **olive-green** sheen. Its face is dark and bare, and the snout is long like a dog's. The males have a mane on the head and shoulders and large canine teeth. They can weigh more than 20 kilograms and are almost twice as heavy as the females. The tail looks as if it were bent in the middle.

Olive baboons live in a broad band from Mali in West Africa to Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania. They are found in **savannas**, open woodland, steppes and even in mountains. This gives them the largest range of all baboons. At night they like to sleep on tall trees or rocks, where they are safe from predators.

Baboons are **omnivores** and very adaptable. They eat grasses, roots, fruit, seeds and tubers. In addition they eat insects, eggs and sometimes small mammals such as young antelopes. Because they are so clever, in some areas they also raid fields and rubbish tips.

Olive baboons live in **troops** made up of several males, many females and their young. In a group there is a clear pecking order. Grooming each other, called **picking lice**, strengthens the friendships between the animals. The females usually stay in the group they were born in for their whole lives, while the males leave as young adults.

The name recalls **Anubis**, the jackal-headed god of the dead of the ancient Egyptians. The sacred baboon of the Egyptians, however, was a relative, the hamadryas baboon, which was linked with the god Thoth. In Ethiopia olive baboons and hamadryas baboons meet and sometimes have young together. In all, six species of baboon are distinguished.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large monkey from Africa that lives on the ground and has a long snout.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A larger group of monkeys that live and travel together.
The order of who is stronger in a group and gets to eat first.

gewusst: A troop of olive baboons can number more than 100 animals.
Baboons communicate with many different sounds, facial expressions and gestures.
When a baboon yawns and shows its canine teeth, it is often a threat.

teile.einleitung: Macaws are large, brightly coloured parrots from Central and South America with long tails and powerful beaks. They include the hyacinth macaw, the largest flying parrot in the world. With their loud calls and bright colours they are among the best-known birds of the rainforest.
wichtigste: Macaws are long-tailed parrots of the New World and belong to the tribe Arini.
Six genera are usually counted as macaws.
Typical is bare or hardly feathered facial skin.
Like all parrots, they have two toes pointing forwards and two pointing backwards.
In the species of the genus Ara, males and females look almost the same.
The hyacinth macaw is the largest flying parrot in the world.
Many macaw species are threatened by deforestation and the animal trade.

abschnitte.text: Macaws have colourful plumage in red, blue, yellow or green and a long, pointed tail. A typical feature is the bare or hardly feathered **facial skin** around the eyes. Their strong, curved beak can crack even hard nuts. The toes are arranged in **pairs**: two point forwards and two point backwards. In the species of the genus Ara, both sexes look almost the same.

Macaws live from Mexico to Argentina. Most species live in **tropical rainforests**, some also in savannas and palm groves. In Peru and Brazil, dozens of macaws often gather at clay walls on river banks and eat soil there. The minerals in the soil probably help them to neutralise poisons from unripe fruit.

Macaws are counted in the **tribe Arini**, the long-tailed New World parrots within the true parrots. Usually six genera are distinguished, including Ara, Anodorhynchus and Cyanopsitta. Well-known species are the scarlet macaw, the blue-and-yellow macaw and the red-and-green macaw. The name “Ara” comes from an Indigenous language of South America and imitates the call of the birds.

The **hyacinth macaw** from the genus Anodorhynchus is the largest flying parrot in the world. It grows to around 1 metre long and can weigh up to about 1.7 kilograms. Its plumage is cobalt blue, and only a ring around the eye and a strip of skin under the beak glow yellow. Only the flightless **kakapo** from New Zealand is heavier. The hyacinth macaw lives mainly in the Pantanal in Brazil and eats hard palm nuts.

Macaws mostly live in pairs, which often stay together for life. They nest in **tree holes** or rock crevices and usually lay two to three eggs. Several pairs often join together in flocks and fly over the forest calling loudly. Macaws can live to a great age, sometimes more than 50 years in human care.

Many macaw species are threatened by the clearing of forests and the illegal **animal trade**. Around the year 2000 the Spix's macaw was considered extinct in the wild. Thanks to breeding programmes, Spix's macaws could be released again in Brazil from 2022. International trade in macaws is strictly regulated by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES, also called the Washington Convention).

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with a curved beak and gripping feet that can often imitate sounds.
A group of closely related genera in the classification of living things.
A group of very closely related species.
Two toes pointing forwards and two pointing backwards, as in all parrots.

gewusst: Macaws use their foot like a hand and hold food to their beak with it.
The Spix's macaw became known around the world through the animated film “Rio”.
The beak of a hyacinth macaw is so strong that it can crack coconuts.

teile.einleitung: Aquaculture means deliberately raising fish, shellfish, crustaceans or algae in tanks, ponds or net pens. You can think of it as farming under water. Today about half of all fish eaten around the world already come from such farms.
wichtigste: Aquaculture is the farming of water animals and water plants.
Farmed species include salmon, trout, carp, prawns and mussels.
Perch are raised not only in lakes but also in fish farms with recirculating water systems.
Worldwide, about half of the fish eaten now come from aquaculture.
China is by far the biggest producer.
Aquaculture can relieve the pressure on the seas, but it also brings environmental problems.
Quality labels help shoppers to recognise responsibly farmed fish.

abschnitte.text: In **aquaculture**, animals and plants that live in water are fed and looked after by people. The word comes from the Latin “aqua” for water and “cultura” for cultivation. There are farms in fresh water, for example for trout and carp, and in the sea, for example for salmon and mussels. Algae are also grown in large quantities.

There are different kinds of fish farm. In **ponds**, carp grow up almost as they do in nature. In the sea, salmon swim in large **net pens** off the coast, for example in Norway. In closed **recirculating systems** the water is cleaned and used again and again, so that hardly any fresh water is needed.

In Switzerland mainly **trout** are farmed, often in facilities beside cool, clean streams. Perch are raised not only in lakes but also in fish farms with recirculating water systems. In the Tropenhaus Frutigen in the Bernese Oberland, sturgeon live in water that comes out warm from the Lötschberg Base Tunnel, and caviar is obtained from their eggs. Even so, most of the fish eaten in Switzerland come from abroad.

Because many seas are overfished, aquaculture is becoming more and more important. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), around 2022 for the first time more water animals were farmed than caught. **China** produces more than half of all farmed fish in the world. India, Indonesia, Vietnam and Norway are also important countries.

When very many fish live in a small space, diseases and parasites can spread quickly. Medicines are then sometimes used, and these get into the water. For prawn farms, large areas of **mangrove forest** were cut down in Asia. Quality labels such as ASC or organic show that stricter rules for the environment and animal welfare apply to a farm.

begriffe.erklaerung: The farming of fish, shellfish, crustaceans or algae by people.
A fish farm in which the water is cleaned and used again and again.
A large net cage in the sea or a lake in which fish are kept.
When more fish are caught than can grow back.

gewusst: More than 2,000 years ago the Chinese were already keeping carp in ponds.
In the Middle Ages, monasteries in Europe built fish ponds so that they could eat fish during Lent.
Part of the feed for farmed salmon consists of fishmeal, which is made from wild-caught fish.

teile.einleitung: The Asiatic lion is a population of lions that today lives only in the west of India. In the past lions also roamed through the Near East and even south-eastern Europe. Today India is the only country outside Africa where there are still wild lions.
wichtigste: In India there is still a small population of lions outside Africa.
The lions live in the state of Gujarat around Gir National Park.
In a count in 2025 about 890 Asiatic lions were counted.
Around 1900 there were only a very few left, perhaps about 20 animals.
Asiatic lions have a smaller mane and a fold of skin along the belly.
Strict protection has allowed the population to recover.
Zurich Zoo keeps Asiatic lions.

abschnitte.text: Asiatic lions are a little smaller than many African lions. The males usually have a shorter, looser **mane**, so that their ears remain clearly visible. A lengthways fold of skin on the belly is typical. A male weighs about 160 to 190 kilograms, a female considerably less.

In the past lions lived from Greece through Turkey and the Near East to India. Through hunting they disappeared in most countries. Today they live only in the state of **Gujarat** in the west of India, around **Gir National Park**. In the count of 2025 there were about 890 animals, after about 670 in 2020.

Asiatic lions live in prides that are usually smaller than in Africa. Often females live together with their young, while the males form groups of their own and join them only for mating. They hunt mainly deer such as the **chital** and the sambar, as well as wild boar. Sometimes they also kill cattle belonging to the herders who live in the area.

Around 1900 only a very few lions were left, estimates speak of about 20 animals. The Nawab of Junagadh, to whom the area belonged, put them under protection. In 1965 the Gir protected area was founded. Because all the lions live in one region, however, an epidemic could be dangerous, and so settling them at a second place is being discussed.

In India the lion is an important **symbol**. The national emblem of India shows the Lion Capital of the emperor Ashoka with four lions. In Europe, Asiatic lions are kept in zoos in a **breeding programme**. In Switzerland they live in Zurich Zoo in a facility modelled on the Gir forest.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the animals of a species that live together in a certain area.
A group of lions that lives and hunts together.
A large protected area for nature and animals.
The long hair on the head and neck of male lions.

gewusst: In the Gir area, lions and herders with their cattle have lived close to each other for a long time.
In ancient times there were also lions in Greece.
Genetically, the Indian lions are closely related to the lions of West and Central Africa.

teile.einleitung: Flat-backed millipedes are a large group of diplopods, that is, millipedes with two pairs of legs per body ring. Typical are the side extensions of the body, which look like flat plates. They live hidden in damp leaf litter and help to break down dead plants.
wichtigste: Flat-backed millipedes are diplopods with plate-like extensions on the sides of the body.
Their scientific name is Polydesmida.
With several thousand species they are the largest order of diplopods.
Flat-backed millipedes have no eyes.
Many species defend themselves with poisonous hydrogen cyanide.
They eat rotting plant parts and are important for the soil.

abschnitte.text: Flat-backed millipedes belong to the **diplopods**, a group of the millipedes. In diplopods almost every body ring carries two pairs of legs. The flat-backed millipedes form the order **Polydesmida** and, with several thousand species, are the largest group of diplopods. They occur on all continents except Antarctica.

Typical of flat-backed millipedes are the side extensions on the body rings, which stick out like flat plates or wings. These extensions are called **paranota** and make the back look flat and band-like. Adult animals usually have about 20 body rings. Flat-backed millipedes have no eyes and find their way with their antennae.

Flat-backed millipedes live in the damp **leaf litter**, under stones, bark and in rotting wood. There they eat rotting leaves and other plant material. In this way, like woodlice and earthworms, they help to form humus. They need moisture and avoid dry, sunny places.

Many flat-backed millipedes have small glands on their sides from which they release a smelly liquid when in danger. In many species this produces **hydrogen cyanide**, a strong poison that scares off ants, spiders and other enemies. The native species, however, are harmless to people. Even so, you should wash your hands after touching them.

Young flat-backed millipedes hatch from eggs with only a few body rings and three pairs of legs. With every **moult** new rings and legs are added. Some species build a small chamber of soil for moulting. In Central Europe and in Switzerland the **flattened flat-backed millipede** is a common species that grows to about two centimetres long.

begriffe.erklaerung: A millipede in which almost every body ring carries two pairs of legs.
Side, plate-like extensions on the back of flat-backed millipedes.
A very poisonous substance that some animals produce for defence.
A layer of fallen leaves on the forest floor.

gewusst: In Thailand there lives a bright pink flat-backed millipede that is called the dragon millipede.
No millipede really has a thousand legs, flat-backed millipedes usually have only about 30 pairs of legs.

teile.einleitung: Antarctica is the region around the South Pole, with the iciest continent on Earth. Almost everywhere lies a thick ice sheet, and it is colder than anywhere else in the world. Even so, penguins, seals and whales live on its coasts, for example most emperor penguins.
wichtigste: Antarctica is the continent around the South Pole.
At about 14 million square kilometres it is larger than Europe.
Around 98 per cent of its area is covered with ice.
The lowest temperature on Earth was measured here, minus 89.2 degrees.
Emperor penguins live almost only in Antarctica.
No one lives there permanently, only researchers in stations.
The Antarctic Treaty protects the continent for peace and research.

abschnitte.text: **Antarctica** includes the continent of Antarctica around the South Pole and the surrounding seas. The continent is about 14 million square kilometres in size, which is about 340 times as big as Switzerland. It is surrounded by the **Southern Ocean**. In winter the sea freezes all around, and the sea ice almost doubles the area. Antarctica should not be confused with the Arctic at the North Pole.

Around 98 per cent of Antarctica is covered by an **ice sheet**, which is more than four kilometres thick in places. About 70 per cent of the Earth's fresh water is locked in this ice. In 1983 minus 89.2 degrees was measured at the Russian Vostok station, the lowest air temperature ever recorded. Because it snows so little, the interior of Antarctica counts as a **cold desert**. If all the ice melted, sea level would rise by many metres.

On land it is too cold for almost all animals, so most live on the coasts and in the sea. The **emperor penguin**, at over a metre tall, is the largest penguin. It breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter on the sea ice, and the male keeps the egg warm on his feet for about two months. Other residents are Adélie penguins, Weddell seals, leopard seals and whales. The basis of the food chain is **krill**, a small crustacean that lives in huge swarms.

abschnitte.titel: Discovery and the race to the Pole
abschnitte.text: Only in 1820 did sailors see the Antarctic continent for the first time. On 14 December 1911 the Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** was the first to reach the South Pole. The Briton Robert Falcon Scott arrived a good month later and died with his companions on the way back. The man from Basel, **Xavier Mertz**, also took part in an expedition and died in Antarctica in 1913. A glacier there bears his name.

Nobody lives in Antarctica permanently, but researchers work in about 70 research stations. In summer there are a few thousand people there, in winter only about a thousand. The **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959 lays down that the continent may only be used and explored peacefully, and Switzerland joined it in 1990. Mining is forbidden, and animals and plants are strictly protected. Drill cores from the ice reveal what the Earth's climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large piece of land, such as Africa, Europe or Antarctica.
A huge, thick layer of ice that covers a whole land.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that serve as food for many whales, seals and penguins.
A base where scientists live and carry out research.

gewusst: There are no polar bears in Antarctica, they only live in the Arctic at the North Pole.
At the South Pole the sun rises only once and sets only once a year.
Antarctica is the continent with the greatest average height, because of the thick ice.

teile.einleitung: The asp viper is a venomous snake that also occurs in Switzerland. Besides the adder, it is the only venomous snake in the country. It is shy, lives on sunny, stony slopes and bites only when it feels threatened.
wichtigste: The asp viper is one of the two venomous snakes of Switzerland.
The other venomous snake of Switzerland is the adder.
Typical is its slightly upturned snout tip.
It has vertical, slit-shaped pupils.
It lives on sunny, stony slopes in the Jura, the Alps and Ticino.
Its young are born alive.
It is protected in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The asp viper usually grows to 60 to 75 centimetres long and has a stocky body. Its colour varies a lot: grey, brown, reddish or almost black. On its back it has dark crossbands or spots. Typical are the slightly upturned **snout tip** and the **vertical pupil**, which is round in harmless native snakes.

The asp viper lives in south-western Europe, mainly in France, Italy and Switzerland. It likes warm, sunny places with stones, rocks, dry-stone walls and bushes. In Switzerland it occurs in the **Jura**, in the Valais, in the western Alps, in the Bernese Oberland and in **Ticino**. In the mountains it climbs to over 2,000 metres.

The asp viper hunts mainly **mice** and other small mammals, sometimes also lizards. It lies in wait for its prey and bites in a flash. The venom works quickly, after which it follows the animal by its scent trail with its tongue. Like all snakes, it swallows its prey whole.

Mating takes place in spring, after **hibernation**. The asp viper does not lay eggs, the young develop inside the mother's body. In late summer, usually 4 to 10 young snakes are born alive. At birth they are already about 20 centimetres long and already have venom.

The asp viper is shy and usually flees before you see it. Bites are rare and happen almost only when it is picked up or accidentally trodden on. A bite is painful and must be treated by a doctor, but deaths are extremely rare in Switzerland. After a bite you should stay calm, call the emergency number 144 or **Tox Info Suisse** on 145, and go to hospital.

In Switzerland all reptiles are protected, including the asp viper. Here it counts as endangered, because its habitats are becoming overgrown with bushes or built over. Dry-stone walls and open scree slopes are especially important for it. When walking in its area, sturdy shoes and long trousers make sense.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of venomous snakes with long, movable fangs.
The dark hole in the middle of the eye through which light enters.
Crawling animals with scaly skin such as snakes, lizards and tortoises.
A long period of rest in winter in which animals use hardly any energy.

gewusst: Fewer than ten species of snake live in Switzerland, but only two of them are venomous.
Snakes smell with their forked tongue.
Young asp vipers shed their skin for the first time soon after birth.

t85todg.t: Bambi, a Life in the Woods

teile.einleitung: “Bambi, a Life in the Woods” is an animal novel by the Austrian writer Felix Salten from 1923. It tells of the life of a young roe deer buck in the forest, from childhood to adulthood. Through Walt Disney's animated film, Bambi became world famous.
wichtigste: Bambi is a book by Felix Salten that appeared in 1923.
The main character in the book is originally a roe deer.
The story shows the life of a young roe buck in the forest with all its dangers.
In the book, man appears as the greatest threat to the animals.
In 1942 Walt Disney brought out a famous animated film.
In the Disney film the roe deer became an American white-tailed deer.
Felix Salten spent his last years in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: The novel **Bambi** appeared as a book in Vienna in 1923, after it had already been printed in a newspaper. The author **Felix Salten** was actually called Siegmund Salzmann and was a well-known Viennese journalist and writer. The book was quickly translated into many languages. It is regarded as one of the best-known animal novels in the world.

Bambi is a young **roe buck** who is born in a clearing in the forest. He learns from his mother what dangers there are and how to survive in the forest. In time he meets other animals, loses his mother to a hunter and has to become independent. An old, wise stag, the old Prince, shows him how to live alone and carefully.

Salten describes the forest very exactly and lets the animals talk to one another. Man is called only **He** by the animals and appears as a dangerous hunter. The book is therefore not only a children's story, but also a serious tale about life and death in nature. Many readers also understand it as a call to respect animals and nature.

In 1942 the animated film **Bambi** by Walt Disney came to the cinemas. Because audiences in the USA did not know European roe deer, Bambi became a **white-tailed deer** in the film. The film added funny supporting characters such as the rabbit Thumper and made the story more suitable for children. Since then many people think first of a fawn when they hear Bambi.

Felix Salten was of Jewish origin, and the National Socialists banned his books. In 1938 he fled from Vienna and moved with his wife to **Switzerland**. He lived in Zurich until his death in 1945. There he wrote more animal books, for example a sequel with the title Bambi's Children.

begriffe.erklaerung: A longer story in which animals are the main characters.
A small species of deer in Europe, the male is called a roe buck.
An American species of deer with a white underside to its tail.
A film made of many drawn pictures that are shown quickly one after another.

gewusst: The name Bambi probably goes back to the Italian word bambino for child.
In the German-speaking world the Bambi is also a well-known media award in the form of a golden roe deer.
Felix Salten also wrote the book “Perri, the Youth of a Squirrel”, which was also filmed by Disney.

teile.einleitung: Autotomy means that an animal voluntarily throws off a part of its body in order to save itself. It is best known in lizards, which lose their tail when a predator grabs it. Often the lost part grows back afterwards.
wichtigste: Autotomy is the self-shedding of a body part for protection.
Lizards such as the sand lizard shed their tail when attacked and flee.
The slow worm can also lose its tail when attacked by a predator.
The shed tail goes on wriggling and distracts the enemy.
The regrown tail is called a regenerate and is usually shorter and without full bones.
Crabs, spiders and harvestmen can also shed legs.

abschnitte.text: The word **autotomy** comes from Greek and means roughly self-separation. The animal deliberately separates a body part, usually a tail or a leg. This happens when an enemy grabs the animal by this body part. In this way the animal can escape, even if it loses something for it.

In many lizards the tail vertebrae have a built-in **breaking point**, that is, a weak spot where they break easily. When a predator holds the tail fast, certain muscles contract and the tail comes away. Blood vessels close at once, so the animal hardly bleeds. The shed tail twitches for a while and so distracts the attacker.

After shedding, a new tail grows back in lizards, which is called **regeneration**. The new part is called a **regenerate** and is usually shorter and a different colour. It no longer contains real vertebrae, but only a tube of cartilage. In the slow worm often only a short, blunt stub grows back.

In Switzerland you can watch autotomy in the **sand lizard**, the wall lizard and the common lizard. The slow worm, a legless lizard, can also lose its tail when it is grabbed by a cat or a bird, for example. That is why you should never touch lizards by the tail. Harvestmen in the garden like to shed a leg when in danger.

Autotomy saves lives in many cases, but it also has disadvantages. Lizards store **fat reserves** in the tail, which are lost when it is shed. Without a tail they keep their balance less well and are often at a disadvantage when looking for a partner. In addition, regrowing costs a lot of energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The independent shedding of a body part in order to escape.
A prepared weak spot where something breaks off easily.
The regrowing of lost body parts.
The regrown body part, for example a new lizard tail.

gewusst: Some geckos can shed their tail several times in their lives and grow a new one.
Starfish can shed arms, and in some species a whole new starfish grows from a single arm.
A shed lizard tail can go on wriggling for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: A worker is a female honeybee who does all the jobs that need doing in the bee colony. She cleans, feeds, builds, guards and collects nectar and pollen. Without the thousands of hard-working workers a bee colony could not survive.
wichtigste: Workers are female bees who normally do not lay eggs themselves.
Most of the bees in a colony are workers.
They do all the jobs in the hive and outside.
Depending on her age, a worker takes on several different tasks.
In summer a worker lives for only about 4 to 6 weeks.
Winter bees, on the other hand, live for several months.
With the waggle dance, foragers show other bees good sources of food.

abschnitte.text: A bee colony consists of one **queen**, a few hundred drones and many thousands of workers. In summer a strong colony often has 30,000 to 50,000 bees. Workers are females whose ovaries are not fully developed. They are a little smaller than the queen and the male **drones**.

In the course of her life a worker has several tasks, a different one depending on her age. Young bees first clean the honeycomb cells, then as **nurse bees** they feed the larvae. Later they build new combs with wax from their wax glands and turn nectar into honey. Only in the last weeks of their lives do they fly out as **foragers**. Older bees that become too old to fly still help in the hive as guards or cleaners.

Foragers fly up to several kilometres to visit flowers. They carry the sweet nectar to the hive in their honey stomach. They carry the pollen as little balls, called **pollen baskets**, on their hind legs. In doing so they pollinate many plants, which is very important for fruit and vegetables.

When a forager has found a good source of food, she dances the **waggle dance** on the comb in the hive. The direction of the dance shows the direction of the food source in relation to the sun. The length of the waggling tells how far away it is. This bee language was decoded by the researcher Karl von Frisch, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1973.

In summer the bees work so hard that they live for only about 4 to 6 weeks. In autumn, on the other hand, **winter bees** hatch, which live for several months. In winter they form a dense cluster and warm the queen by shivering their flight muscles. If a worker stings a person, her barbed sting stays stuck in the skin and she dies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female bee that works in the colony and normally does not lay eggs.
A male honeybee.
A young worker that feeds the larvae.
A structure of six-sided wax cells in which brood, honey and pollen are stored.
A dance with which bees show each other the way to sources of food.

gewusst: For a 500 gram jar of honey, bees have to fly many thousands of kilometres.
A worker produces only about a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.
Whether an egg becomes a worker or a queen is decided by the food: a queen larva gets royal jelly for the whole of her larval life.

teile.einleitung: Species extinction means that species of animals and plants disappear from the Earth for ever. This has always happened, but today species are dying out much faster than before because of the influence of humans. Experts therefore speak of one of the greatest challenges of our time.
wichtigste: When an animal species disappears from the whole world, it is called extinction.
When a species is destroyed by humans, it is called extermination.
In the history of the Earth there were five great mass extinctions.
Today species are dying out much faster than they naturally would.
The most important cause is the destruction of habitats.
According to a world report from 2019, about a million species are threatened with extinction.
An extinct species never comes back.

abschnitte.text: A species counts as **extinct** when not a single living individual of that species exists any more. If it is deliberately destroyed by humans, this is called **extermination**. Species extinction is actually a natural process, because almost all species that have ever lived have died out. The problem, though, is that today it is happening much faster than normal.

In the history of the Earth there were five great **mass extinctions**, in which very many species disappeared in a short time. The biggest happened about 252 million years ago at the end of the Permian, when probably more than three quarters of all species died out. The best known was 66 million years ago, when a giant asteroid hit the Earth. Then the dinosaurs disappeared, with the exception of the birds.

The most important cause is the destruction of **habitats**, for example when rainforests are cut down or bogs are drained. Added to this are overfishing, hunting and poaching. Environmental poisons, climate change and introduced animals and plants that push out native species are also dangerous. The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, **IPBES**, estimated in 2019 that about a million species are threatened with extinction.

The **dodo**, a flightless bird from the island of Mauritius, was wiped out in the 17th century. The passenger pigeon was once one of the commonest birds in North America, but the last one died in 1914 in a zoo in Cincinnati. The thylacine from Tasmania disappeared in the 1930s. Many other species die out unnoticed before they have even been discovered.

In Switzerland, too, about a third of the animal and plant species studied are endangered. Bear, wolf, lynx and ibex had at times disappeared from here altogether. Some have returned or have been reintroduced. Especially threatened today are species of wetlands, dry meadows and many **insects**.

Every species has its job in the **ecosystem**, the interplay of all living things. Bees and other insects, for example, pollinate our fruit trees. If too many species disappear, the whole web of living things can start to wobble. Protected areas, nature-friendly farming and climate protection help to slow down species extinction.

begriffe.erklaerung: When not a single living individual of a species exists any more.
Extinction of a species that was caused by humans.
A time in which very many species die out in a short period.
The variety of all living things and habitats on Earth.

gewusst: It is estimated that more than 99 per cent of all species that ever lived on Earth have died out.
The last passenger pigeon was called Martha.
Some experts say that we are right now in the sixth mass extinction in the history of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Avermectins are active substances against worms and other parasites that originally come from a soil bacterium. They help millions of people and animals, but can also harm useful insects such as dung beetles. Their discovery was honoured with the Nobel Prize.
wichtigste: Avermectins are substances against parasites such as worms, mites and lice.
They were obtained from the soil bacterium Streptomyces avermitilis.
The best-known active substance in this group is ivermectin.
Satoshi Ōmura and William C. Campbell received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015 for the discovery.
In veterinary medicine, grazing animals such as cattle, sheep and horses are wormed with them.
Residues in the dung of treated animals can harm dung beetles and their larvae.

abschnitte.text: The Japanese researcher **Satoshi Ōmura** collected soil samples in the 1970s in order to find new bacteria. In a sample from Japan he discovered a bacterium that was later called **Streptomyces avermitilis**. The American William C. Campbell found out that substances from this bacterium kill worms in animals. These substances were called avermectins.

Avermectins attack the nerves and muscles of invertebrates such as worms, mites and insects. The parasites are paralysed as a result and die. In mammals and people they work much more weakly in the usual amounts, because these nerve sites are built differently and are protected by the **blood-brain barrier**. That is why they can be used as a medicine.

From the avermectins the active substance **ivermectin** was developed. It is used mainly in Africa and South America against river blindness, a disease caused by tiny threadworms that can make people blind. Since 1987 a pharmaceutical company has been giving the medicine away in large amounts for this disease. For this achievement Ōmura and Campbell received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.

In farming, cattle, sheep, goats and horses are wormed with avermectins. They also help against mites, lice and warble flies. In dogs and cats related substances are used against parasites. Part of the active substance, however, is excreted again unchanged in the **droppings**.

In the dung of treated animals, residues of the products often remain for days or weeks. Dung beetles, dung flies and their larvae, which live in cowpats, can be harmed or die as a result. Then the **cowpats** are broken down more slowly and the pasture stays dirty for longer. Experts therefore recommend treating animals only when necessary and not all at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives on or in another living thing and harms it.
The best-known medicine in the group of the avermectins.
A tropical disease caused by threadworms that can lead to blindness.
Freeing an animal of worms with a medicine.

gewusst: A teaspoon of garden soil contains millions of bacteria, and from one of them came a Nobel Prize medicine.
The soil sample with the famous bacterium came from near a golf course in Japan.

teile.einleitung: Nurse sharks are easy-going sharks that often lie quietly on the seabed during the day. They only become active at night, when they go hunting. They are usually harmless to people as long as they are left alone.
wichtigste: Nurse sharks form a family of their own with only a few species.
During the day they often lie quietly on the seabed, sometimes in groups.
At night they hunt fish, crabs, squid and mussels.
They suck in their prey with their mouth like a vacuum cleaner.
They have two barbels on their snout for feeling their way around.
The Atlantic nurse shark grows to about three metres long.
Nurse sharks give birth to live young.

abschnitte.text: Nurse sharks have a strong, brown body with a broad head and small eyes. Their mouth sits right at the front, and in front of it hang two fleshy **barbels** that they use to feel along the seabed. The two dorsal fins sit far back. The **Atlantic nurse shark** usually grows to about two to three metres long, occasionally a little larger. Their skin feels rough like sandpaper.

Nurse sharks live in warm, shallow coastal waters, often in **coral reefs**, lagoons and seagrass meadows. The Atlantic nurse shark is found on both sides of the Atlantic and in the eastern Pacific, for example in the Caribbean and off Florida. The tawny nurse shark lives in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. During the day they rest in caves or under rock ledges. Often several animals lie close beside or even on top of one another.

Nurse sharks are **nocturnal**. In the dark they slowly search the seabed. They eat fish, crabs, squid, sea urchins and mussels. With their strong gill muscles they create a powerful suction and simply **suck** their prey in. They can even pull snails out of their shells this way.

Many sharks have to keep swimming all the time so that water flows over their gills. Nurse sharks, however, can actively pump water through their mouth and **gills**. That is why they can lie motionless on the bottom for hours. Small openings behind the eyes, called **spiracles**, also help them to breathe. This saves them a lot of energy.

Nurse sharks are **live-bearing**: the eggs develop inside the mother's body. A female gives birth to about 20 to 30 young, which are already a good 25 centimetres long. Nurse sharks are usually harmless to people. But if they are disturbed or pulled by the tail, they can bite hard and do not let go quickly. Because they are calm, they can also be seen in large show aquariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: Feeler-like threads of skin near the mouth that a fish can use to feel and taste.
An animal that is mostly awake at night and looks for food then.
The breathing organs of fish, which take oxygen from the water.
A small opening behind the eye of many sharks and rays through which water can flow in.

gewusst: Nurse sharks can suck in their prey faster than the eye can follow.
A nurse shark can lie still and breathe at the same time, which many other sharks cannot do.

teile.einleitung: The lesser stag beetle is a black beetle that is closely related to the famous stag beetle. It is much smaller and has no antler-like mandibles, but it is considerably more common. You often find it on rotting wood in woods, parks and gardens.
wichtigste: The lesser stag beetle is closely related to the stag beetle and belongs to the stag beetle family.
Its scientific name is Dorcus parallelipipedus.
It is usually about 2 to 3 centimetres long and matt black.
The males have only short, strong mandibles and no large antlers.
Its larvae develop for several years in rotting hardwood.
In Switzerland it is quite widespread at lower altitudes.

abschnitte.text: The lesser stag beetle, in Latin **Dorcus parallelipipedus**, belongs to the family of **stag beetles**. The large stag beetle is therefore its close relative. Unlike in the stag beetle, however, the mandibles of the males are not lengthened into antlers. You can recognise males by their broader head and the somewhat larger jaws.

The lesser stag beetle usually grows to about 2 to 3 centimetres long. Its body is matt black and looks like a flat, oblong block. The Latin name also points to this, as it recalls a **cuboid**. The antennae are bent and end in a small club made of little plates.

Lesser stag beetles live in deciduous woods, parks, orchards and gardens with old trees. They need **dead wood**, that is, dead, rotting wood from trees such as beech, oak, willow or fruit trees. The adult beetles are about from May to September, mainly at dusk and in the night. During the day they hide under bark or in cracks in the wood.

The female lays her eggs in rotting wood, often in tree stumps on the ground. The white, curved **larvae** eat their way through the decaying wood for two to three years. After that they pupate, and the finished beetle hatches. The adult beetles can overwinter and sometimes live for more than a year.

Lesser stag beetles help to break down dead wood and turn it into soil. This makes them important members of the forest **cycle**.
